sections.title: Background sources cited in PLA Safety Bulletin SB3-25, "Proper Use of VHF
sections.text:
This document summarizes, in plain language, each of the nine sources listed in the "Further Reading" table of the Port of London Authority's Safety Bulletin SB3-25. These are the international, EU-derived, and UK legal and guidance instruments that together set out how VHF marine radio must be used. Each summary is written independently of the source text and is not a substitute for reading the original — links are provided at the end of each section.

---

sections.title: 1. SOLAS Chapter IV — Radiocommunications
sections.text:
**Source:** International Maritime Organization (IMO), International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, Chapter IV
**Link:** https://www.imo.org/en/About/Conventions/Pages/International-Convention-for-the-Safety-of-Life-at-Sea-(SOLAS),-1974.aspx

SOLAS is the core international treaty governing ship safety, and Chapter IV of its Annex deals specifically with radiocommunications. Its purpose is to guarantee that ships covered by the Convention are equipped so they can reliably send and receive distress and safety information, coordinate with each other and with shore authorities in emergencies, and call on organized search-and-rescue services when needed. The chapter also ensures that radio installations across different vessels and shore stations are technically compatible with one another, that they remain functional even after a single equipment failure (i.e., there is built-in redundancy), and that they are properly maintained throughout a ship's operational life.

Chapter IV applies to all passenger ships on international voyages and to cargo ships of 300 gross tonnage or more on international voyages. It underpins the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS), the internationally standardized system of satellite and terrestrial communication procedures used for maritime distress alerting.

The chapter has been substantially revised over time to keep pace with changing technology. A major modernization came into force on 1 January 2024 (via IMO Resolution MSC.496(105)), which updated the GMDSS to reflect the shift away from older systems. Under the revised chapter, ships operating in certain sea areas (A3/A4) are no longer required to carry high-frequency narrow-band direct-printing telegraphy (HF NBDP) equipment for transmitting and receiving distress and safety messages, and NAVTEX/EGC/HF NBDP receivers are no longer automatically mandatory — although owners may retain such equipment voluntarily for receiving maritime safety information. The amendments also broadened recognition of satellite service providers beyond Inmarsat to include other "Recognized Mobile Satellite Service" providers, such as Iridium, where a flag state accepts them.

In UK law, SOLAS Chapter IV's requirements are given direct legal effect through the Merchant Shipping (Radiocommunications) (Amendment) Regulations 2021 (see Section 2 below), and MCA Marine Guidance Note 641 (M) explains how UK-flagged ships and operators should apply it in practice.

---

sections.title: Source:** UK Statutory Instrument, in force from 24 December 2021
sections.text:
**Link:** https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2021/1316/contents/made

This Statutory Instrument is how the UK brings SOLAS Chapter IV into domestic law. It has two main effects. First, it directly imposes the SOLAS Chapter IV radiocommunications requirements on UK ships (and non-UK ships in UK waters) undertaking international voyages. Second, it amends the earlier Merchant Shipping (Radio Installations) Regulations 1998 so that ships on non-international voyages continue to have appropriate radio requirements, while ships covered by the Convention now only need to comply with the 2021 Regulations rather than the 1998 ones.

Structurally, the Regulations are organized into four parts. Part 1 covers general matters: citation and commencement, definitions, which ships the rules apply to, and provisions allowing the Secretary of State to grant exemptions or approve equivalent arrangements where full compliance would be unreasonable or impractical for a particular vessel. Part 2 sets out the basic functional requirement that ships must be able to transmit and receive distress and safety communications. Part 3 deals with the technical detail: performance standards for equipment, requirements for radio installations, watchkeeping obligations, maintenance duties, qualifications for radio personnel, record-keeping, and equipment testing. Part 4 covers enforcement — offences, penalties, and a ship's potential detention if it fails to comply.

A distinctive and important feature of these Regulations is the "ambulatory reference" provision (regulation 7). This means that whenever SOLAS Chapter IV is amended internationally in future, those changes are automatically incorporated into UK law at the same time, without needing a fresh Statutory Instrument each time. This keeps UK requirements permanently aligned with the current international standard.

The Regulations apply, with limited exceptions, to United Kingdom ships wherever they are, and to non-UK ships (including those from countries that haven't ratified SOLAS) while they are in UK waters.

---

sections.title: Source:** Maritime and Coastguard Agency
sections.text:
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mgn-641-amendment-1-m-guidance-on-radiocommunications-under-chapter-iv-of-solas

MGN 641 (M) is the MCA's practical guidance document explaining how shipowners, masters, shipbuilders, and seafarers should interpret and apply the Merchant Shipping (Radiocommunications) (Amendment) Regulations 2021 described above. Rather than creating new legal obligations itself, it is meant to be read alongside the 2021 Regulations to clarify what compliance looks like in practice — and in fact parts of the Note have been given the force of law by the Regulations.

The guidance is structured around eight key topic areas: an introduction to the legal framework; how "recognised satellite service providers" are determined; requirements for radio installation on board; the sources of electrical energy that must be available to power radio equipment (including backup power in case of failure); the performance standards equipment must meet; maintenance requirements to keep radio equipment serviceable; qualifications and duties required of radio personnel on board; and the record-keeping obligations for radio logs.

Because the Regulations incorporate future SOLAS amendments automatically via the ambulatory reference mechanism, the guidance note is periodically reissued or amended (there have been at least one or two amendments since first publication in December 2021) to reflect the latest position and remove ambiguity for those applying the rules day to day.

---

sections.title: 4. Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006
sections.text:
**Source:** UK Public General Act, 2006 c. 36, Parliament of the United Kingdom
**Link:** https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/36/contents

The Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 is the principal UK statute governing the use of radio apparatus of all kinds — not just maritime — including marine VHF sets. It received Royal Assent on 8 November 2006 and largely consolidated earlier wireless telegraphy legislation (including the Wireless Telegraphy Acts of 1949 and 1967) into a single, modernized Act, while also repealing a range of older enactments. It applies across the whole of the United Kingdom.

The Act gives Ofcom its general statutory functions over the radio spectrum, including licensing radio apparatus and enforcing compliance. Two aspects of the Act are directly relevant to the misuse of VHF radio referenced in the PLA bulletin. Section 48 makes it a criminal offence to use wireless telegraphy apparatus to intentionally intercept the contents of a message not intended for the interceptor, or to disclose the contents, sender, or addressee of such a message obtained that way — a provision aimed at protecting the privacy and integrity of radio communications, including on marine VHF channels. Section 116 defines "wireless telegraphy" broadly, in essence covering the transmission or reception of electromagnetic energy up to 3,000 gigahertz used for conveying messages, sounds, or images, or for operating equipment, or for determining position or detecting objects — a definition wide enough to capture VHF, radar, and AIS.

More broadly, operating radio apparatus without the required licence, or in a way inconsistent with licence conditions, is an offence under the Act, and this is the legal basis referenced by the PLA bulletin when it warns that "unnecessary transmission" or "non-standard phrases" on VHF may constitute a breach of the Act. The Act has been amended numerous times since 2006 (for example by the Digital Economy Acts of 2010 and 2017, and the Investigatory Powers Act 2016) to keep pace with changing telecommunications technology and enforcement practice.

---

sections.title: Source:** UK Statutory Instrument, in force from 26 December 2017
sections.text:
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/radio-equipment-regulations-2017

These Regulations set out the technical and safety requirements that radio equipment (including marine VHF sets) must meet before they can legally be placed on the UK market or put into service. They were originally made to implement the EU's Radio Equipment Directive (2014/53/EU) into UK law and have since been adapted for the UK's post-Brexit UKCA (UK Conformity Assessed) marking regime, distinct from the EU's CE marking.

The Regulations' "essential requirements" (broadly in regulation/Article 3) require that radio equipment be constructed so that it protects the health and safety of users and other people (including domestic animals) and property; that it achieves an adequate level of electromagnetic compatibility, meaning it neither causes excessive interference to other equipment nor is itself unduly affected by interference; and that it makes effective use of the radio spectrum so as to avoid causing harmful interference to other radio users — a point directly relevant to why "unnecessary transmission" and "non-standard phrases" on VHF are discouraged, since spectrum efficiency is a legal design and use consideration, not just an etiquette one.

The Regulations place obligations on the various "economic operators" in the supply chain — manufacturers, importers, and distributors — including duties to prepare technical documentation, ensure conformity assessment procedures are followed, cooperate with enforcement authorities, and withdraw non-conforming equipment from the market if concerns are identified. Ofcom has powers to evaluate and act against radio equipment that presents a risk. The Regulations exclude certain categories of equipment from their scope, including some radio amateur and marine equipment governed by separate regimes, and they allow for different requirements in Northern Ireland reflecting its distinct post-Brexit trading arrangements.

---

sections.title: 6. ITU Radio Regulations
sections.text:
**Source:** International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a United Nations specialized agency
**Link:** https://www.itu.int/pub/R-REG-RR

The ITU Radio Regulations are a binding international treaty — technically an integral part of the ITU's Administrative Regulations, which complement the ITU's Constitution and Convention — governing how the global radio-frequency spectrum (from 9 kHz to 300 GHz) and satellite orbits are used and shared among all 193+ ITU member states. They are the foundational document underpinning virtually all national radio law, including the UK's Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006.

The Regulations are revised roughly every three to four years by the World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC) to keep pace with new technology and changing spectrum demand, with the most recent full edition dated 2024. They are published in four volumes: Volume 1 contains the Articles (definitions, technical terms, and substantive rules, organized into chapters and numbered provisions); Volume 2 contains the Appendices (including detailed technical annexes such as those governing distress and safety frequencies); Volume 3 contains Resolutions and Recommendations; and Volume 4 contains ITU-R technical Recommendations incorporated by reference.

Of particular relevance to VHF maritime use, the Regulations define and classify various maritime radio services — the "maritime mobile service" (communication between coast stations, ship stations, and onboard units), the "maritime mobile-satellite service," the "port operations service" (restricted to messages about the operational handling, movement, and safety of ships, explicitly excluding general public correspondence), and the "ship movement service" (similarly restricted to messages about ship movements). This is the direct legal source for the PLA bulletin's requirement that VHF transmissions be strictly relevant to safety of navigation and operational coordination — the ITU treaty itself defines these radio services narrowly and excludes casual or personal messages from them by treaty definition. The Regulations also govern priority of communications (distress and safety traffic takes precedence), secrecy of communications, and the allocation of frequency bands (via the Table of Frequency Allocations in Article 5), which nationally-administered plans such as the UK's must follow.

---

sections.title: Source:** International Maritime Organization, Resolution A.918(22), adopted November 2001
sections.text:
**Link:** https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Safety/Pages/StandardMarineCommunicationPhrases.aspx

The SMCP is a standardized set of English-language phrases developed by the IMO to reduce the risk of misunderstanding in verbal maritime communication, given that English is the internationally recognized working language at sea but is not the first language of most seafarers. It replaced an earlier, narrower document called the Standard Marine Navigational Vocabulary (SMNV), which had been in use since 1977.

The SMCP is organized into two parts. Part A covers essential phrases for external communication (ship-to-shore, shore-to-ship, and ship-to-ship) as well as onboard communication, focusing on navigation and ship handling — this is the part formally required for certification purposes. Part B is a supplementary, non-mandatory set of additional phrases intended to support wider maritime English learning. The phrases cover both routine situations (such as berthing and pilotage) and standard responses for emergencies, and are deliberately built on a simplified subset of English grammar and vocabulary to minimize ambiguity.

Under the STCW Convention (the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers), officers in charge of a navigational watch on ships of 500 gross tonnage or above are required to demonstrate the ability to understand and use the SMCP as part of their certification. While the SMCP is primarily aimed at bridge-to-bridge and bridge-to-shore navigational safety communication rather than being a VHF-specific procedural rulebook, it is the natural companion to the PLA bulletin's requirement for clear, concise, and standardized language on VHF, since ad hoc or idiosyncratic phrasing is precisely what the SMCP was designed to eliminate.

---

sections.title: Source:** Maritime and Coastguard Agency
sections.text:
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mgn-324-mf-amendment-2-navigation-watchkeeping-safety-use-of-very-high-frequency-vhf-radio-and-automatic-identification-system-ais

MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

---

sections.title: 9. Ofcom Ship Radio Licence Guidance
sections.text:
**Source:** Office of Communications (Ofcom)
**Link:** https://www.ofcom.org.uk/manage-your-licence/radiocommunication-licences/ships-radio

This is Ofcom's guidance on the licensing regime for radio equipment carried on ships, covering medium frequency (MF), VHF, high frequency (HF), and ultra-high frequency (UHF) radio equipment, as well as satellite communications, radar, Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacons (EPIRBs), and Search and Rescue Transponders (SARTs). The stated purposes of licensing are twofold: to prevent radio equipment from causing undue interference to other users of the spectrum, and to ensure equipment is operated only by competent, appropriately trained individuals.

Historically a UK "Ship Radio Licence" required annual renewal and a fee, but following a 2005 Ofcom consultation and policy change, ships' radio licences became "lifetime" licences from 1 October 2006 — free of charge, issued electronically, with no fixed expiry date, remaining valid as long as the registered details stay accurate (though licensees must periodically reconfirm their details). A licence is personal to the licensee and does not automatically transfer if a vessel is sold. Separately from the equipment licence, the individual operating the radio needs an operator's qualification — for VHF-only use this is the Short Range Certificate (SRC), obtained via a one-day training course covering radio procedure, etiquette, and use of Digital Selective Calling (DSC); a Long Range Certificate (LRC) is needed for other, longer-range communications equipment.

Operating marine radio equipment without both the required ship licence and a valid operator's certificate is a criminal offence. Ofcom's enforcement team can issue on-the-spot fines, and the maximum penalty on conviction is a £5,000 fine and/or up to six months' imprisonment, with the possibility of forfeiture of any radio apparatus used unlawfully. This is the direct legal underpinning of the PLA bulletin's warning that improper VHF use may lead to penalties enforced by Ofcom.

---

*Note: This document is a set of independent summaries prepared for reference purposes and does not reproduce the source texts. For authoritative, up-to-date, and legally definitive wording, always consult the original documents at the links provided above.*
